verse.text: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word wherever the Greek has one.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers and sisters, as is fitting, because your faith is growing abundantly and the love that every one of you has for one another is increasing,
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women. Since the letter is addressed to the whole community, “brothers and sisters” conveys what the first hearers understood. Many recent translations do the same.

verse.text: so that we ourselves boast about you in the assemblies of God for your endurance and faith in all your persecutions and the afflictions that you are bearing.
This is evidence of God’s just judgment, so that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are in fact suffering,
verse.note: The Greek is a loose phrase in apposition to verse 4, without “this is”, and it does not say exactly what the evidence is. Most interpreters take it to be the Thessalonians’ endurance and faith under persecution. Others take it to be the sufferings themselves, understood as a sign that God’s judgment is already at work and will set things right.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Here and in verse 6 the point is that God judges fairly, so “just” is used. Many translations have “righteous judgment” in verse 5 and “just” or “a righteous thing” in verse 6, although the Greek word is the same.

verse.text: since indeed it is just in God’s sight to repay with affliction those who afflict you
and to give relief to you who are afflicted, along with us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his powerful angels
in flaming fire, dealing out retribution to those who do not know God and to those who do not obey the good news of our Lord Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it now sounds like a religious term or a book title. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

note.term: in flaming fire, dealing out retribution

verse.note: The language of verses 8–9 is drawn from Isaiah in its Greek form: the Lord coming “in a flame of fire” to render retribution (Isaiah 66:15), and people hiding “from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might” (Isaiah 2:10). What Isaiah says of Israel’s God is here applied to the Lord Jesus. “Retribution” is used instead of the traditional “vengeance” because the Greek word denotes the carrying out of justice, not personal vindictiveness.

verse.text: These will pay the penalty of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,

note.term: away from the presence of the Lord
note.traditional: from the presence of the Lord

verse.note: The Greek preposition is simply “from”. It may mean separation (“away from the presence of the Lord”), which is the majority view and is the sense in Isaiah 2:10. It may instead mean source (“destruction that comes from the presence of the Lord”). The nature of the “eternal destruction” itself—unending ruin or final annihilation—is debated and cannot be settled from the wording alone.

verse.text: when he comes on that day to be glorified in his holy ones and to be marveled at among all who have believed—because our testimony to you was believed.
verse.note: “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue, whereas the Greek word is used of all believers as people set apart for God. The parallel with “all who have believed” suggests that believers are meant here, though some interpreters think of angels, as in Psalm 89:7. The phrase could also be rendered “among his holy ones”.

verse.text: To this end we also pray for you always, that our God may count you worthy of his calling and fulfill with power every desire for goodness and every work of faith,

note.traditional: count you worthy, make you worthy

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means “consider worthy”, and that sense matches “counted worthy” in verse 5. Several translations render it “make you worthy”, which fits the following prayer that God would bring their good intentions to completion. That sense is less well attested for this verb.

note.traditional: all the good pleasure of his goodness

verse.note: The Greek is literally “every good pleasure of goodness” and does not say whose it is. Older translations took it as God’s own good pleasure. Most modern interpreters take it as the Thessalonians’ resolve to do good, because it is paired with “work of faith”, which is clearly theirs.

verse.text: so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

note.term: our God and the Lord Jesus Christ
note.traditional: our God and the Lord Jesus Christ

verse.note: In Greek a single article governs both “God” and “Lord Jesus Christ”, so the phrase can be read as “our God and Lord, Jesus Christ”, calling Jesus God. Most scholars think two persons are meant, because “Lord Jesus Christ” often stands without the article as a fixed title and the letter’s opening distinguishes God the Father from the Lord Jesus Christ. The other reading is grammatically possible.

verse.text: Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him,
not to be quickly shaken out of your senses or alarmed, whether by a spirit or by a spoken word or by a letter, as though from us, claiming that the day of the Lord has come.
verse.note: This most likely means a prophetic utterance claimed to be inspired, delivered in the congregation. The three channels named are prophecy, ordinary spoken teaching and a letter. The words “as though from us” may apply to the letter alone or to all three; the Greek leaves this open, and the punctuation here does the same.

The Greek perfect normally means “is present” or “has arrived”, and Paul elsewhere uses the same form for “things present” as opposed to things to come. The King James rendering “is at hand” (that is, near) is hard to support from usage. Most modern translations have “has come”, though how anyone could have thought the day was already here remains debated.

verse.text: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,
verse.note: The Greek sentence breaks off: it gives the condition (“unless the rebellion comes first…”) but never states the main clause. Nearly all translations supply “that day will not come” from verse 2, and that is done here.

In the period the word was used both for political revolt and, in the Greek Old Testament, for religious defection from God. “Rebellion” covers both. Whether Paul has in view a defection among God’s people or a general human revolt against God is disputed, and the definite article suggests an event the readers had already been told about.
The earliest manuscripts read “lawlessness”; many later ones read “sin”, which is the reading behind the King James Version. “Lawlessness” also fits verses 7 and 8, where the same root recurs.
“Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone who belongs to or is destined for something. The phrase means the one doomed to destruction. The related verb appears in verse 10 as “those who are perishing”.

verse.text: who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the sanctuary of God, proclaiming himself to be God.
verse.note: Greek has one word for the whole temple complex and another, used here, for the inner building where the deity dwells. Most English versions render both as “temple”; this translation uses “sanctuary” for the second. Whether Paul means the Jerusalem sanctuary literally, or uses the image for a claim to divine status, is debated.

verse.text: Do you not remember that I used to tell you these things while I was still with you?
And now you know what is restraining him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.
verse.note: The Greek has no object, and “him” is supplied. The restrainer is a thing (neuter) here and a person (masculine) in verse 7. Paul had explained it in person, and its identity is now unknown: proposals include the Roman empire and emperor, the preaching of the good news, an angel, or God. A minority take the verb as “hold sway” and read it as a hostile power. “Now” may also go with the participle (“what is now restraining”).

verse.text: For the secret power of lawlessness is already at work; only the one who now restrains will do so until he is out of the way.
verse.note: Most versions have “the mystery of lawlessness”. In the Jewish Greek of the period the word meant a secret, something hidden until disclosed, not a puzzle. Here the secret is the subject of “is already at work”: lawlessness is operating out of sight before the lawless one is openly “revealed”. “Secret power” brings out that contrast.

verse.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of his coming.
verse.note: The wording echoes Isaiah 11:4 in the Greek version, where the coming king strikes the earth with the word of his mouth and kills the wicked with the breath of his lips. The Greek word can mean “spirit” or “breath”; the allusion settles it as “breath” here.

The verb means to strip something of its force or put it out of operation; it is not the ordinary word for destroying. The King James Version and several modern versions have “destroy”, while others have “bring to nothing” or “annihilate”. The point is that the lawless one’s power collapses at the mere appearance of Jesus.

verse.text: The coming of the lawless one is by the working of Satan, with all power and with lying signs and wonders,
and with every kind of wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they did not accept the love of the truth so as to be saved.
And for this reason God sends a delusion to work in them, so that they believe the lie,
so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in wickedness.

But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers and sisters loved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and faith in the truth.
verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two readings that differ by a single letter in Greek: “as firstfruits” and “from the beginning”. The Greek text translated here reads “firstfruits”, the first portion of a harvest offered to God. Many translations follow the other reading, and the question is not settled.

verse.text: To this he called you through our good news, so that you might obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, including public proclamations. “Gospel” is now a purely religious term or the name of a book. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions you were taught, whether by spoken word or by our letter.
Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal encouragement and good hope by grace,
encourage your hearts and strengthen them in every good deed and word.
Finally, brothers and sisters, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run swiftly and be honored, just as happened among you,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and here the whole congregation is in view. “Brothers” alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. The generic singular in verses 6 and 15 is likewise rendered “brother or sister.” Several modern translations do the same.

The verb means to hold in high honor or to praise. Applied to a message, it means that the message is received with the respect it deserves, as it had been in Thessalonica. “Be glorified” is the older rendering; some modern translations also use “honored.”

verse.text: and that we may be rescued from perverse and evil people, for not everyone has faith.
But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil one,” that is, Satan) or neuter (“evil” in general). Most modern translations choose “the evil one,” partly because of the letter’s interest in Satan’s activity in chapter 2. “From evil,” as in the KJV, remains possible. The same adjective describes the “evil people” of verse 2.

verse.text: We have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will go on doing what we command.
May the Lord direct your hearts toward the love of God and the endurance of Christ.

note.term: the love of God and the endurance of Christ
note.traditional: the love of God and the patient waiting for Christ (KJV)

verse.note: Both phrases are ambiguous in Greek. “The love of God” may be God’s love for them or their love for God. “The endurance of Christ” may be the endurance Christ himself showed, the endurance he gives, or steadfast waiting for him. The rendering leaves this open as the Greek does; most interpreters favor God’s love for believers and Christ’s own endurance as the model.

verse.text: Now we command you, brothers and sisters, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to keep away from every brother or sister who lives irresponsibly and not according to the tradition they received from us.

note.traditional: disorderly (KJV); in idleness / idle (many modern versions)

verse.note: The word describes failing to keep to an expected order or duty; in documents of the period the related verb is used of people who neglect their obligations, such as apprentices who miss work. “Disorderly” now suggests rowdiness, and “idle” fits the context of verses 10–12 but is narrower than the word itself. The same word family is rendered “irresponsible” in verse 7 and “irresponsibly” in verse 11.

Manuscripts differ between “they received” and “you received,” and a few have “he received.” The Greek text followed here reads “they received,” the plural referring loosely to every such brother or sister. The sense is hardly affected.

verse.text: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not irresponsible among you,
nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying; rather, in labor and toil we worked night and day so as not to burden any of you.
It is not that we lack the right, but we wanted to give you ourselves as an example to imitate.
verse.note: This is the entitlement of those who preach the gospel to be supported by their hearers. Paul sets out that right at length in 1 Corinthians 9 and there too explains why he chose not to use it.

verse.text: For even when we were with you, we used to give you this command: if anyone is unwilling to work, they should not eat either.
verse.note: The Greek says “is not willing,” so the rule targets refusal to work, not inability to work or to find work. The older rendering “would not work” meant the same but is now easily misread. The origin of the saying is uncertain; it resembles proverbial sayings about work, but no exact earlier parallel has been identified.

verse.text: For we hear that some among you are living irresponsibly, not busy working but busybodies.

note.traditional: working not at all, but are busybodies

verse.note: The Greek is a play on words: the two participles share the same root, roughly “not working but working around,” that is, meddling in what is not their concern. “Not busy … but busybodies” reproduces the pun, as several English versions do.

verse.text: Such people we command and urge in the Lord Jesus Christ to work quietly and eat their own bread.
But as for you, brothers and sisters, do not grow weary of doing what is right.
If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, take note of that person and do not associate with them, so that they may be ashamed.
Yet do not regard them as an enemy, but warn them as a brother or sister.
Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with you all.
This greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. It is the mark in every letter; this is how I write.

note.traditional: the token / the sign in every epistle

verse.note: Ancient letters were commonly dictated to a secretary, and the sender often added the closing lines in his own handwriting. Paul points to his handwriting as the mark of a genuine letter. This is probably connected with the concern in 2:2 about a letter falsely claiming to come from him.

verse.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
